items: Route subscriptions to the socket or SSE transport
Route everything else to plain HTTP
One client, two links, chosen per operation
Auto-merge happens only on a known `id` plus changed fields
Same-id merge is the entire mechanism, nothing more
A new list item needs `updateQuery` or a cache modifier
The cache cannot guess which lists an addition belongs to
Deletion must evict the entity AND filter every cached list
`subscribeToMore` binds a stream to an existing query
Initial fetch and live updates share one cache entry
And one loading state, so the UI stays coherent
Events between the query snapshot and an active stream vanish
The UI misses them silently, with no error anywhere
Never fetch-then-subscribe; always subscribe-then-fetch
On reconnect, refetch the base query, do not assume continuity
Treat every reconnect as a possible data gap
Send a cursor or `Last-Event-ID` to replay from a point
Replay only exists if the backend is durable

blocks.title: Strict Mode double-subscribe
blocks.text: React Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development, opening and closing the subscription twice. Confirm teardown ran before blaming the server.

items: At-least-once delivery brings dupes and out-of-order events
Carry a monotonic version or timestamp per entity
Drop any write older than what the cache already holds
Optimistic result plus the server echo double-applies
Dedupe on entity id and version to kill both
Correct more often than teams assume
Subscriptions buy latency, pay in permanent ops complexity
A 5-second poll averages 2.5s staleness
If the product tolerates that, sockets add zero user value
1,000 users at 10s = 100 req/sec, trivially cacheable
Stateless, cacheable, load-balanced with no extra work
Survives deploys and network changes without logic
Debuggable with `curl` and ordinary access logs

blocks.text: `ETag` plus `If-None-Match` makes an unchanged poll nearly free: no body, no rendering, no serialization.

items: Update rate high AND freshness under a second matters
Chat, collaborative cursors, live prices, multiplayer state
Irregular but urgent: an alert, a finished long job
Polling burns requests waiting on a moment that may never come
Something changing twice a day does not need an open socket
Smart polling: fast when focused, slow when backgrounded
Stop entirely on `document.hidden`, often cuts 80% of traffic
Notify-then-fetch: event says 'changed', client refetches cached query
SSE-only broadcast for one-way public data, outside GraphQL
Anonymous consumers scale on CDN cache, never on sockets

blocks.title: The arithmetic
blocks.text: If time between events is greater than the poll interval, poll. If events per minute per subscriber exceed 6 and freshness matters, subscribe.

items: Publishing inside the transaction races the commit
Subscribers refetch and read pre-commit state
Publish after commit, ideally via a transactional outbox
Subscribing per request, not per connection, multiplies broker subs
It climbs until the broker's client limit is hit
No `resolve` plus a mis-keyed payload gives `messageAdded: null`
No error is raised, which is why it costs hours
Some servers kill the whole stream on one event's error
Catch inside execution, emit a payload-level error instead
Subscriptions are invisible to HTTP-based tooling
APM traces, request logs, status dashboards all show nothing
Unbounded rate on a hot topic pins the CPU on JSON
Throttle or batch events server-side before delivery
N+1 inside a resolver runs on every single event
Query load = N+1 times event rate times subscriber count

lines: # raw stream first, never debug via the UI

items: `wscat` for raw WebSocket protocol inspection
Load test with k6 or Artillery: connections, not req/sec
Integration test: subscribe, mutate, assert first N results
Assert teardown actually released the broker subscription
Chaos: kill a broker node, confirm resync not silent connect

blocks.title: Three rules to keep
items: Publish thin events, after commit
Authorize per event, not just at connect
Assume the client missed something; make resync cheap

blocks.title: Final judgment
blocks.text: Reach for a subscription only when sub-second freshness is a real product requirement. Otherwise poll with ETags and spend the complexity budget elsewhere.

caption.text: Part 2 of GRAPHQL SUBSCRIPTIONS. Most teams reach for GraphQL subscriptions and inherit a broker, a reconnect state machine, and a cache reconciliation problem — to save 2.5 seconds nobody asked for. This handbook walks the whole stack: the two-phase execution model, graphql-transport-ws message by message, pub/sub backends from EventEmitter to Kafka, fan-out cost math, and the exact arithmetic that tells you to just poll instead. Ten pages, every gotcha we have paid for.
